findings.title: [P1] Restore interval cancellation in the polling disposer
findings.body: After callers invoke the disposer returned by `startPolling`, `refresh` continues running every second. Repeated lifecycle cycles accumulate timers and duplicate work, and the live interval can prevent a Node.js process from exiting. Preserve the timer handle and clear it during disposal.

findings.title: [P2] Remove the message listener during disposal
findings.body: Calling the disposer returned by `attach` now leaves `handler` registered. Messages can therefore invoke callbacks after teardown, while repeated attach/dispose cycles retain closures and produce duplicate processing.

findings.title: [P1] Restore interval cancellation in the returned disposer
findings.body:
After `startPolling()` returns, invoking its disposer no longer stops the interval. `refresh` continues indefinitely after teardown, and in Node.js the live timer can prevent process termination. Repeated start/stop cycles also accumulate concurrent pollers.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore message-listener removal during teardown
findings.body:
Calling the disposer returned by `attach()` leaves `handler` registered. Subsequent messages therefore invoke callbacks after their lifecycle has ended, while repeated attachment cycles accumulate duplicate handlers and retained state. This affects any EventEmitter-compatible socket once teardown occurs.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore removal of the message handler during cleanup
findings.body:
Calling the returned disposer no longer unregisters `handler`. Any subsequent `"message"` event still invokes supposedly disposed handlers, causing stale callbacks, duplicate processing after reattachment, and listener leaks.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Clear the polling interval during cleanup
findings.body:
After `startPolling()` returns, invoking its disposer leaves the interval active. The callback continues firing every second and, in Node.js, the referenced interval can prevent process shutdown.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener revocation on cleanup
findings.body:
When a caller invokes the returned cleanup during session or authorization teardown, the listener remains active. A remote peer retaining the socket can continue sending messages to a handler that the application believes was revoked, potentially causing unauthorized state changes or retaining sensitive session data.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Cancel polling timers on cleanup
findings.body:
Each call now leaves a permanent one-second timer and retained callback. In an environment where untrusted requests or repeated lifecycle events can start and then dispose polling, timers accumulate without bound, enabling process memory and CPU exhaustion.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore interval cancellation in the polling disposer
findings.body:
Every `startPolling` call now creates an interval whose handle is discarded. Calling the returned cleanup function cannot stop it, so Node processes remain alive and repeated start/cleanup cycles retain callbacks and perform unbounded duplicate work every second.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Remove the message listener when disposing an attachment
findings.body:
On any long-lived socket, calling the returned disposer leaves the handler registered. Repeated attach/dispose cycles therefore retain handler closures and increase work per message linearly, potentially triggering listener-limit warnings and memory growth.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
